extracted.intended_audience: aspiring comic-book creators / beginner sequential artists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for breaking a written comic script into pages and panels, planning page layouts with thumbnails/sketches, and designing readable, well-paced comic book pages for print or web.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break script into pages and panels
rubrics_metrics.description: Print out the script and read through it, marking where it might be a good idea to cut to a new page. Count the pages you broke it down to and judge length/pacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark script where page breaks feel natural; ensure something vaguely interesting happens on every page; avoid overstuffing a page since it must be broken into panels. Use this step to check total length (too long/short) and adjust as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cliffhanger endings for page breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: End a page JUST where something exciting is about to happen (a character opens a cellar door, an explosion is implied, etc.) to keep readers' interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply cliffhanger endings selectively (not on every page) to maintain momentum. The technique encourages readers to turn the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cramming too much information on a page
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful how much information you cram into every page, because it must be divided into panels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a page has too many distinct beats or actions, break it across more pages or redistribute beats into fewer panels. Overloaded pages make drawing harder and storytelling less clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit panels per page
rubrics_metrics.description: More than 6 or 9 panels per page is usually very hard on the eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple 9-panel grid is a safe starting point. If you need variation, adjust sizes or reduce number of panels; too many small panels create a hectic feel and are visually fatiguing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit speech balloons per frame
rubrics_metrics.description: More than three speech balloons in one frame makes the story hard to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep dialogue per panel concise; if a scene requires many lines, break dialogue across panels or pages to preserve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control pacing with panel size and dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Calm/quiet scenes are usually done with big pictures and not a lot of dialogue; bigger and more detailed panels tend to slow down reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide desired pacing scene-by-scene: use larger panels for beats you want the reader to linger on, and smaller/faster panels for brisk action. Leave room for key images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use thumbnails (small sketches) before full pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Do small sketches (thumbnails) to get a feel for layout and pacing before committing to larger, detailed drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thumbnails are fast and reveal pacing/layout problems early (e.g., needing extra panels). They save time and grief compared to working directly on finished page art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text pages before drawing to ensure dialogue fits
rubrics_metrics.description: TEXT pages before drawing for two reasons: (1) to be sure dialogue fits in speech balloons, and (2) because it's boring—get it out of the way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay out all dialogue and captions to check space and balloon placement before sketching so you don't have to retrofit text into finished art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include an establishing shot to orient the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Start scenes with an establishing shot (e.g., a skyline, a house) so readers immediately know where the action is taking place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good establishing shot lets you simplify backgrounds in subsequent panels while maintaining reader orientation; it saves time and helps story clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide variation in panels and within frames
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure every panel is not the same: vary panel size, composition, and internal framing (close-ups, silhouettes, full-figure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variation keeps pages visually interesting and can save drawing time (e.g., use silhouettes after you've established characters). Match panel choice to emotional beats (some reactions need detail; others can be silhouettes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard grids and experiment cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: A 9-panel grid is reliable; you can vary size/number of panels for effect, but proceed with caution when experimenting with irregular layouts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open panels work well for single-subject images; skewed/irregular panels can convey chaos but may complicate reading order. Test experimental grids in thumbnails first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use splash pages, bleed, and split panels intentionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Splash pages (large panels across a spread), bleed (art to the edge of the page), and split panels (one image fragmented across panels) are layout tools with specific effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Splash pages and bleeds emphasize impact—if printing, extend art over the page edge for bleed. Split panels can suggest time passing. Use these techniques where they serve the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: If printing, allow for bleed and safe-zone margins
rubrics_metrics.description: When using bleed for print, have your art extend OVER the edge of the page and leave a safe zone so important elements aren't trimmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add roughly an extra centimeter (or printer-specified bleed amount) beyond the print size; create a template with a scaled-down safe area layer to visualize margins and avoid trimmed content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain clear reading order
rubrics_metrics.description: Always be aware of reading order; the page should flow naturally so the reader doesn't have to stop and decide which panel or balloon to read next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design panels and balloon placement to guide the eye; confusing order hurts storytelling. Test reading flow in thumbnails to ensure it’s intuitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave room for key images and planned beats
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have key images or moments in mind, leave space for them in your layouts—they may be primary motivations for making the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan pages so important images get adequate size and placement; if a beat is central, avoid cramming it into a tiny panel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep script flexible for artists; don't over-prescribe panels
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing scripts, don't describe every panel in excruciating detail—leave room for interpretation and changes in panel size/composition by the artist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific panel-by-panel scripting can feel restraining for artists. Thumbnails and the sketching phase often reveal storytelling snags that the script didn’t foresee; collaboration and flexibility improve the final page.
